name: AI and Authorship
title: AI and Authorship
answer: AI and authorship covers the questions of who or what counts as an author when artificial intelligence systems produce text, images, code, music, or other works. It spans copyright law, academic integrity, publishing ethics, creative credit, and the attribution of ideas. The field examines both the legal status of AI-generated output and the practical norms that govern how humans and machines are credited. It also looks at how authorship is verified, disputed, and recorded in research and industry.

sections.body: AI and authorship covers the questions of who or what counts as an author when artificial intelligence systems produce text, images, code, music, or other works. It spans copyright law, academic integrity, publishing ethics, creative credit, and the attribution of ideas. The field examines both the legal status of AI-generated output and the practical norms that govern how humans and machines are credited. It also looks at how authorship is verified, disputed, and recorded in research and industry.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of computational and institutional infrastructure. Large language models and generative systems produce the raw output, while provenance tools such as watermarking and metadata standards track where content came from. Publishing platforms, preprint servers, and repositories hold the resulting works and their attribution records. Version control systems and audit logs help document who changed what and when. Institutional review boards and editorial policies also form part of the operating environment.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Researchers in this area combine legal analysis, computational text analysis, and empirical studies of publishing practice. They compare model outputs against human writing, test attribution and watermarking tools, and survey how journals and conferences handle AI contributions. Case studies of disputed authorship and plagiarism investigations are common. The site's 13608 extracted claims from research works provide a structured evidence base for mapping arguments across the literature.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in AI and authorship center on copyright ownership, liability for harmful or false content, and the integrity of the scholarly record. Provenance is a key concern, with efforts to track the origin of text, images, and data through metadata, watermarks, and disclosure statements. Risks include misattribution, plagiarism, fabricated citations, and the erosion of trust in published work. Governance responses range from updated journal policies and institutional codes to emerging regulations and court decisions. The field also grapples with how to assign responsibility when an AI system generates problematic output.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more formal disclosure requirements and technical standards for provenance. Courts and legislatures are beginning to clarify how existing law applies to AI-generated works, though many questions remain open. Publishers and research institutions are experimenting with new attribution models, including explicit statements of AI use. Tooling for watermarking and content credentials is likely to become more common. Debates over whether AI can be an author, or only a tool, will continue to shape policy and practice.
